assumptions.summary: Convection only; no radiation or evaporation; constant ambient air.
One-dimensional flow and uniform cross-sections preserve selected 3-D extensive effects.
Bather heat is prescribed as a spatial source fraction.

contributions.summary: Build a uniform control-volume energy balance.
Solve a forced one-dimensional heat equation.
Add convection and finite differences with stability bounds.
Separate temperature target error and uniformity metrics.
Use PID forcing and distributed input heat.
Return the technical chain to a user-facing bath recommendation.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Density, conductivity, and specific heat are assigned from literature.
Natural-convection regime is selected through Grashof/Reynolds estimates.
Nominal geometry, temperatures, flow, and transfer coefficients support one-factor comparisons.

edges.handoff: Steady energy and boundary coefficients supply the transient heat equation.
Analytical heat solution identifies missing bulk motion, motivating convection-diffusion.
Numerical fields provide average-error and uniformity metrics for comparison.
Comparison metrics become the PID error signal and control target.
Average-temperature forcing is extended to spatially distributed inlet control.
Heat-map improvement becomes the final user strategy.

feedbacks: Sensitivity and control stages return to the same target-error and uniformity metrics before the final recommendation.

independent_extensions.summary: Run grid-refined three-dimensional CFD with measured bath temperature fields.
Tune PID gains under actuator saturation and sensor noise, then report robust stability.
Replace prescribed bather heat fractions with pose/contact-area measurements.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A separate audience letter may aid communication; award status is not causal evidence.

language_observations.summary: Summary names three models, comparison, PID control, and user strategy.
Overview moves from physical difficulty to questions, route, comparison, and future work.
Metrics are defined before model ranking.
Final letter translates control and distribution into direct action.

models.summary: A steady state treats the bath as a uniform control volume with inlet, outlet, and ambient convection.
A Fourier-based heat equation with time-dependent Neumann boundaries and heat generation is transformed and solved analytically.
The numerical model adds a convection term to the heat equation and uses explicit finite differences with stability criteria.
The paper separates average-temperature error from standard deviation and varies geometry, soap, input, flow, and bather factors.
PID gains convert target error into a forcing function for inlet temperature and flow.
The second PID stage redistributes input heat over spatial positions rather than only regulating average temperature.
The final recommendation combines PID temperature control with continuous, distributed inlet water and states model boundaries.

results_trace.summary: Average target error and standard deviation become shared metrics.
Input temperature and flow change response directionally.
Distributed inlet heat improves uniformity while conserving water.

section_map.summary: State the physical target and the three-model route before derivation.
Compress the route from physical question to implementable control.
Turn an everyday cooling problem into a bounded staged work plan.
Stabilize the symbol vocabulary before equations.
Make the reduction explicit and attach each assumption to the later model.
Build a steady control-volume baseline from geometry and heat-transfer coefficients.
Add time dependence and source terms to capture bather heat and changing boundaries.
Translate the convection-diffusion PDE into a finite-difference algorithm with explicit stability limits.
Separate nominal inputs, computed outputs, and verification plots.
Vary geometry, soap, input water, flow, and bather factors using common metrics.
Evaluate each model using explicit positive capability and transfer boundary.
Close the technical chain with a controlled strategy and conditions.
Translate equations and simulations into an audience-specific practical recommendation.
Close the paper with provenance without adding reusable technical claims.

limitations: All 44 rendered pages were reviewed through six contact sheets; equation-heavy pages 12-18 and 22-26 and control pages 35-40 were inspected at full resolution.
Text extraction damages mathematical glyphs, so rendered equations are authoritative.
The paper reports no raw Matlab files, grid refinement, empirical temperature field, actuator limits, or uncertainty analysis.

deliverables: Model bathtub temperature in space and time.
Compare steady, analytical, and numerical heat-transfer models.
Evaluate geometry, soap, input temperature, flow rate, and bather factors.
Regulate average temperature with PID control.
Improve spatial uniformity through distributed heat input and communicate a practical strategy.
task_reconstruction.reconstruction_limit: No separate official Problem A statement was located; the paper's explicit scenario and path-derived A classification are retained.
task_reconstruction.source: Summary Sheet, Introduction, model sections, Model Comparison, Control Theory, Final Remarks, and user letter

title: Beneath the Surface: A Thermal-Fluid Analysis of a Hot Bath
unresolved_questions: What grid, timestep, code, and convergence checks reproduce the numerical maps?
How are PID gains selected and bounded under real faucet constraints?
How do radiation, evaporation, and tub material change the recommendation?
How does bather position and motion alter the distributed heat source?
Can the uniformity metric be validated with spatial temperature sensors?

verification.summary: Boundary-case heat maps verify qualitative analytical behavior.
Finite-difference heat map demonstrates convection-diffusion evolution.
Objective and standard-deviation curves expose model behavior.
Gain-specific response shows rise time and oscillation.
Optimized PID map shows distributed input strategy.

weaknesses.summary: Radiation, evaporation, material transients, and flow disturbance are omitted.
Natural-convection coefficients use rough nominal film values.
Grid refinement and raw code are absent.
Heat source fractions proxy body movement.
Gain tuning and actuator limits are incomplete.
No empirical closed-loop bath trial is reported.

writing_logic.summary: State the physical target and the three-model route before derivation. | Establish {field model} and choose a strategy balancing {uniformity}, {target tracking}, and {water use}.
Compress the route from physical question to implementable control. | Describe {baseline}, {analytical model}, {numerical model}, then compare and control {metric}.
Turn an everyday cooling problem into a bounded staged work plan. | When {physical system} loses {resource}, define {questions}, then map {models}, {comparison}, and {future work}.
Stabilize the symbol vocabulary before equations. | Define {symbol} as {quantity} with {unit} before using it in {equation/model}.
Make the reduction explicit and attach each assumption to the later model. | Assume {geometry/physics} so that {full problem} reduces to {tractable problem}, while retaining {effect}.
Build a steady control-volume baseline from geometry and heat-transfer coefficients. | Define {domain}, estimate {properties}, and derive {steady balance} before transient extensions.
Add time dependence and source terms to capture bather heat and changing boundaries. | Extend {baseline} with {time-dependent boundary/source} and solve {analytical heat equation}.
Translate the convection-diffusion PDE into a finite-difference algorithm with explicit stability limits. | Discretize {space/time}, state {update rule}, and enforce {stability criterion}.
Separate nominal inputs, computed outputs, and verification plots. | Insert {nominal parameters}, run {solver}, and compare {field/metric} against {reference or expected trend}.
Vary geometry, soap, input water, flow, and bather factors using common metrics. | Vary {factor}, recompute {metric}, explain {mechanism}, and state {bounded advice}.
Evaluate each model using explicit positive capability and transfer boundary. | For {model}, retain {strength} and bound {limitation} before future extension.
Close the technical chain with a controlled strategy and conditions. | Given {comparison}, select {control strategy} under {assumptions} and state {decision boundary}.
Translate equations and simulations into an audience-specific practical recommendation. | For {user}, use {action} because {mechanism}, subject to {caveat}.
Close the paper with provenance without adding reusable technical claims. | Cite {source} for {parameter/method} and preserve the evidence boundary.
